CausalChain: Hypoxia in HCC → HIF-1α upregulation → Increased expression of ENTPD2 on tumor cells → Enhanced conversion of extracellular ATP to AMP → Elevated adenosine levels in TME → Recruitment and activation of MDSCs → Suppression of CTL activity → Tumor immune evasion; Inhibition of ENTPD2 → Reduced adenosine accumulation → Decreased MDSC infiltration → Restoration of CTL function → Improved efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors
Hypothesis: Inhibition of ENTPD2 in hypoxic hepatocellular carcinoma will attenuate adenosine‐mediated recruitment of MDSCs and alleviate CTL suppression, thereby enhancing the antitumor efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint blockade therapies.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) that compromises the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors. Recent studies have highlighted the role of metabolic enzymes in shaping this microenvironment. We propose that hypoxia‐driven upregulation of ectonucleoside triphosphate diphosphohydrolase 2 (ENTPD2) on HCC cells converts extracellular ATP into AMP, leading to increased local adenosine production. This metabolic shift promotes the accumulation and immunosuppressive function of myeloid‐derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), thereby inhibiting cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) activity. Targeted inhibition of ENTPD2 is hypothesized to restore ATP/adenosine balance, reduce MDSC recruitment, and potentiate the efficacy of PD‐1/PD‐L1 blockade in HCC.
